sentenceSets.sentence: His insolence toward those with less institutional standing made his deference toward those with more visibly inconsistent.

answerChoices.reasoning: The sentence is careful to say the behavior appeared only toward people of lower standing while a different manner appeared toward people of higher standing; brashness is an indiscriminate boldness that would not switch off in front of superiors.
Disdain names a feeling he holds inwardly, but the sentence turns on something observers could see and set beside his outward deference.
Condescension is a patronizing warmth that sits comfortably alongside good manners, so it would not have made his politeness upward look inconsistent.

Arrogance describes an inflated estimate of oneself, which could just as easily accompany the deference he showed upward; the sentence needs something that contradicts that deference rather than something compatible with it.
Impatience would be provoked by delay or slowness, yet the sentence sorts his behavior strictly by the other person's rank.
Bluntness is a plain way of speaking that many would excuse as honesty; nothing that neutral would expose his courtesy toward superiors as a pose.
Indifference implies he paid junior colleagues no attention at all, but the sentence describes a manner directed at them.
Hostility suggests active enmity toward particular people, while the sentence describes a pattern applied to a whole category defined only by standing.
Courtesy toward junior colleagues would make his courtesy toward senior ones perfectly consistent, which is the opposite of what the sentence reports.
Humility would leave nothing for observers to contrast with his deference; the sentence needs a clash between two treatments.
Reverence is close in spirit to the deference the sentence places on the other side of the contrast, so it cannot be what undercuts it.

sentenceSets.sentence: The apprentice's insolence—correcting the master mid-lecture and then smirking at the correction—cost him a place he had waited three years to earn.

answerChoices.reasoning: Flippancy is a failure to take a matter seriously, yet the sentence shows him following the lecture closely enough to catch an error in it.
Defiance requires an order or rule that was refused, and the sentence reports no instruction he disobeyed, only how he addressed someone senior.
Presumption would be fully accounted for by the correction itself; the smirk the sentence adds shows relish in the slight, which overstepping one's place does not explain.
Audacity frames an act as nerve or daring, but the consequence recorded here—losing a place he had waited three years for—marks the behavior as an offense given rather than a risk taken.
Obstinacy would require him to hold a position against pressure, while the sentence shows a single interruption and a smirk, not a refusal to yield.
Vanity concerns an excessive regard for one's own appearance or gifts, and the sentence measures him by how he treated the master, not by self-regard.
Sarcasm operates through words that mean their opposite, but the correction he offered was apparently accurate and meant literally.
Self-importance describes an inflated sense of one's own consequence, which would not by itself explain a punishment aimed at how he treated his superior in public.
Deference would be the behavior the master wanted, and it could not have cost the apprentice the place he was waiting for.
Modesty is incompatible with interrupting a lecture to correct the person giving it.
Timidity would have kept him silent, yet the sentence has him speaking up mid-lecture and smirking afterward.

sentenceSets.sentence: Colonial administrators recorded every act of insolence in their ledgers, treating a slow answer or an unbowed head as evidence that the population was growing ungovernable.

answerChoices.reasoning: Insubordination requires a chain of command and a refused order, but the two examples given—a slow answer and an unbowed head—involve no instruction at all.
Truculence implies aggression or an appetite for a fight, while the behaviors catalogued here are passive: slowness and posture rather than menace.
Recalcitrance names a stubborn refusal to be managed, yet the ledger entries record matters of bearing and manner, not instances of noncompliance.
Irreverence concerns treating something sacred or dignified lightly, and what the administrators wrote down was conduct toward officials, not mockery of anything held holy.
Resentment is an inward grudge, and a ledger can only record acts that were performed in front of someone.
Sullenness would cover the slow answer but not the unbowed head, which asserts something rather than withholding it.
Apathy would make a population easier to govern, not harder, which is the inference the administrators are said to draw.
Unrest describes a condition spread across a population, but the ledger entries are individual acts performed by particular people in particular encounters.
Obedience would be exactly what the administrators wanted and no reason to fear the population was slipping from their control.
Loyalty would reassure the administrators rather than fill their ledgers with warning signs.
Diligence concerns care in work, which has nothing to do with the posture and tone of reply being recorded here.
